subsystems.name: Gas supply
subsystems.role: delivers the raw materials the microbes eat: carbon dioxide, hydrogen, oxygen and mineral nutrients.
parts: CO2 feed (captured air or industrial off-gas)

subsystems.name: Bioreactor loop
subsystems.role: the fermentation vessel where bacteria grow — a liquid loop with strong gas mixing, because hydrogen dissolves poorly in water.

subsystems.name: Electrolysis and power
subsystems.role: makes the hydrogen and oxygen from water using renewable electricity.

subsystems.name: Gas recycling and safety
subsystems.role: recovers unused hydrogen and CO2 and keeps the mixture away from explosive conditions.

subsystems.name: Harvest and drying
subsystems.role: separates the cells from the water and turns them into a stable powder.

subsystems.name: Formulation and quality control
subsystems.role: turns the powder into a food ingredient and proves it is safe.

buildSteps.title: Produce the gases
buildSteps.detail: Renewable electricity runs an electrolyser that splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. This is the single biggest energy input.

buildSteps.title: Capture the carbon
buildSteps.detail: Carbon dioxide is pulled from the air with direct air capture, or taken from an industrial flue stream, then cleaned and compressed.

buildSteps.title: Culture the microbes
buildSteps.detail: A starter culture of hydrogen-oxidising bacteria, such as Cupriavidus necator, is grown in small seed vessels and stepped up in volume until it is large enough to inoculate the main reactor.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the medium
buildSteps.detail: The reactor is filled with water plus mineral salts supplying nitrogen, phosphorus and trace metals, and is cleaned or sterilised so competing organisms cannot take over.

buildSteps.title: Run the bioreactor
buildSteps.detail: Hydrogen, oxygen and CO2 are fed into the loop. The bacteria burn hydrogen for energy and fix the CO2 into biomass, doubling every few hours. Hydrogen and oxygen form an explosive mixture, so the gas composition and gas-transfer rate are the central engineering problem — enough gas must dissolve to feed the culture without entering a flammable regime.

buildSteps.title: Harvest continuously
buildSteps.detail: Broth is drawn off and spun or filtered to concentrate the cells into a wet paste, while water and unused gas are recycled.

buildSteps.title: Break and dry the cells
buildSteps.detail: The cell walls are disrupted so the protein is digestible, then the paste is spray dried into a fine powder that is roughly two-thirds protein with fats and carbohydrates.

buildSteps.title: Formulate and clear
buildSteps.detail: The powder is blended into foods and must pass novel-food safety review in each market before sale, backed by feeding trials and allergen testing.

prerequisites.why: electricity is the main cost and the main emissions source; the process only makes climate sense if the power is clean.
they supply the hydrogen and oxygen that feed the bacteria.
direct air capture works but is still expensive; industrial flue gas is cheaper but ties the plant to a fossil site.
industrial fermentation is mature, but transferring hydrogen and oxygen safely at large volume is not.
a new ingredient needs approval market by market before it can be sold.

pathway.milestone: pilot and first small commercial plants, with one market (Singapore, 2022) having approved the ingredient
pathway.unlocks: proof that the process works outside the lab and can be eaten.

pathway.milestone: larger plants co-located with cheap renewable power and a CO2 source
pathway.unlocks: falling cost per kilogram as reactors scale and electrolysers get cheaper.

pathway.milestone: approvals in the EU, US and other large markets
pathway.unlocks: real commercial volumes instead of demonstration batches.

pathway.milestone: integration with direct air capture and surplus renewable power
pathway.unlocks: protein production decoupled from farmland, weather and season — an earlier attempt at single-cell protein in the 1970s failed on cost, and this route depends on not repeating that.
